topic: Why SMS two-factor codes are risky
hook: Your two-factor text message codes can be stolen without anyone touching your phone.

blocks.narration: Your two-factor text message codes can be stolen without anyone touching your phone. It is called a SIM swap.
blocks.visual: Sleek dark UI with a glowing SIM card sliding out of one phone and into another, neon accents

blocks.narration: First, a criminal gathers personal details about you online, then contacts your mobile carrier while pretending to be you.
blocks.visual: Glassy panels of scattered personal info assemble into a fake identity card

blocks.narration: If the carrier is fooled, your phone number moves to a SIM card the criminal controls. Your phone suddenly loses service.
blocks.visual: The victim's phone shows no bars while another phone lights up with the same number

blocks.narration: Now every login code sent by text goes straight to them. Email, banking, and social accounts can fall one after another.
blocks.visual: Glowing account icons tumble like dominoes toward the criminal's phone

blocks.narration: Better options exist. Authenticator apps generate codes on your own device, and security keys or passkeys are even stronger.
blocks.visual: A glowing authenticator code ticks on the real phone, a small hardware key beside it

blocks.narration: Move your most important accounts over first, starting with email, since your email can reset the password on almost everything else.
blocks.visual: The email icon glows brighter than the others, linked by lines to every account

blocks.narration: Then call your carrier or check its app for a port-out PIN or number lock. It makes these swaps much harder.
blocks.visual: A padlock snaps shut around the SIM card

blocks.narration: Set this up tonight, it takes ten minutes. And share this with someone who uses text codes for everything.
blocks.visual: The phone glows green with full signal and a shield icon as the camera pulls back

cta: Do it tonight, and share this with someone who uses text codes for everything.

captions.hook_line: Your 2FA text codes can be stolen without touching your phone 📱
captions.body: In a SIM swap, a criminal convinces your carrier to move your number to their SIM and then receives your text-message codes. Authenticator apps, security keys or passkeys are stronger, and many carriers offer a port-out PIN or number lock.
